questions.prompt: Complete this line from the poster of a reading club: "The more you read, ……… you know."
questions.explanation: The structure needs the word the in front of both comparatives, and that doubled the is what ties the two changes together — drop it from the second half and the sentence stops being a parallel change at all. The superlative is impossible here, since only two things are being compared and neither is the highest of a group. And much more is an ordinary intensified comparative, which would need something to be compared with, whereas this half of the sentence compares itself with nothing: it simply follows the first half up.

questions.prompt: Your book asks what means Lois E. Hole uses to support her argument for libraries, and its instruction says "tick the correct answer(s)". Which pair does she actually use?
questions.explanation: She reasons from cause to consequence — books are expensive, therefore libraries matter; a country needs literate people, therefore schools deserve support — and she closes on a saying set between quotation marks, which is quotation. Statistics are the easiest to eliminate: there is not a single figure anywhere in the five paragraphs, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing. And nothing is imagined, since every step of the text argues about the real world. The plural in the instruction is the clue that two boxes have to be ticked rather than one.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 24, three things killed the pop single. Which trio does the first paragraph name?

options.text: The internet, MTV and mobile phones.
The internet, the cassette and the CD.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph names exactly those three and no others: the internet, MTV and mobile phones. Radio, television and cinema belong to an older world, and the article uses radio to explain the opposite point — that there was once nowhere else to hear a song, so you had to buy it. The cassette and the CD are formats rather than causes, and the CD in fact appears as the cheap album that competes with the single. And compilation albums, ringtones and downloads are all real causes, but they arrive in paragraphs four and five, not in the first.

options.text: I must go to the bank because I haven't got no money left.
I must go to the bank because I haven't got any money left.
I must go to the bank because I haven't got some money.
I must go to the bank because I have got no any money at all left.

questions.explanation: The verb is already negative in haven't got, and after a negative verb English uses any, which gives haven't got any money left. Adding no on top of that negative verb produces a double negative, which is the commonest written mistake of the whole lesson. some after a negative verb is simply the wrong member of the pair, since some belongs to affirmatives, offers and questions that expect yes. And piling no and any together is impossible in any position: they are two answers to the same question, and a sentence takes one or the other.

questions.prompt: A limerick is a funny poem of five lines. Which rhyme scheme does it follow?
questions.explanation: Lines one, two and five rhyme with each other and are the longer ones; lines three and four rhyme with each other and are short and quick, which gives A A B B A. Alternating the rhymes from the first line onwards would break the pair in the middle, and it is precisely that short central pair that gives the limerick its rhythm. Grouping three A rhymes at the start and two B at the end puts the short lines last, where the joke belongs. And beginning with a single A leaves line one with no partner until the very end, which no limerick does.
